idiom_name: entity struct with an EntityId newtype, keyed in a store; PartialEq by id
implementation_notes: Rust has no object identity for owned values and #[derive(PartialEq)] compares all fields, so the idiom is to make identity explicit: declare a typed id (a newtype over Uuid or a handle integer), keep entities in a collection keyed by that id (HashMap<CustomerId, Customer> or an arena) and implement PartialEq/Hash on the id only, or expose fn same(&self, other: &Self) -> bool. Methods take &mut self, so a single owner hands out mutable access and the borrow checker rules out two simultaneous mutable views of one entity - the aliasing bug other languages must catch at runtime is prevented at compile time. This is the default Rust realization for domain models; Rc/Arc are only needed when an entity must be genuinely shared between owners.
pitfalls: #[derive(PartialEq, Hash)] on the entity struct compares and hashes every field, so a renamed customer stops being equal to itself; derive those on the id type and implement them by hand for the entity.

Cloning an entity to satisfy the borrow checker creates a second copy with the same id; keep one owned copy in the store and hand out &mut borrows, or share it deliberately with Rc<RefCell<_>>/Arc<Mutex<_>> and accept the runtime borrow panics or lock overhead.
Implementing PartialEq on a subset of fields can break the equivalence-relation requirements that Eq, Hash and collections rely on (the standard library documents this); identity is the safe subset.

variants.name: Shared entity behind Rc/Arc, identity by allocation
variants.idiom_name: Rc::ptr_eq / Arc::ptr_eq identity over a shared allocation
variants.implementation_notes: When several owners must hold the same entity - shared graphs, concurrent services, observer-style references - wrap it in Rc (single-threaded) or Arc (thread-safe) and test identity with Rc::ptr_eq/Arc::ptr_eq, which are true only for handles pointing at the same allocation; mutability then needs RefCell or Mutex because the borrow checker no longer enforces exclusivity. Note that == on Rc/Arc is value equality of the inner type, not identity, so the identity check must call ptr_eq explicitly. Use this variant sparingly: it buys shared identity at the cost of runtime borrow panics (RefCell) or lock overhead and deadlock risk (Mutex), and the durable identity is still the stored id once the entity outlives the process.
pitfalls: Rc::ptr_eq/Arc::ptr_eq ignore value equality: two separately constructed entities with the same id are not identical, so the id remains the durable identity across serialization and reconstruction.
RefCell borrow panics and Mutex poisoning or deadlocks replace compile-time aliasing errors; hold borrows and locks for the shortest possible scope and never across a callback.
Arc::ptr_eq compares value pointers including metadata, so for trait objects the comparison can be false for the same allocation in some cases; compare concrete types or ids where that matters.
